activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: The word hypothesis comes from ancient Greek and literally means 'putting or placing under'.
story:
The gymnasium smelled like hot glue and floor wax, and the air was so humid that Easton's display board curled slightly at the corners. He smoothed it flat and taped it down again, then stood back and stared at the word he had lettered across the top in blue marker: HYPOTHESIS. His project asked which brand of battery kept an LED burning longest, and his guess had been that the expensive brand would win. It had not. The cheap battery was still glowing on his table after nineteen hours, and the fancy one had died at midnight.

Kiaan leaned over from the next table, where his volcano oozed baking-soda foam onto a tray. "You look like your dog died."

"My hypothesis was wrong," Easton said. He said the word slowly, like a stone in his mouth. Last month he had nearly skipped writing one at all. Mr. Gagnon had circled the empty spot on his rough draft and written one word back: why? Easton had stayed up late that night making something up, just to fill the box, and he had envied Kiaan, whose volcano needed no guessing at all. Now the guess he had invented to please a teacher was the thing being proven wrong in public, under fluorescent lights, with judges walking the aisles.

Amina wandered over with her clipboard, judging sheet and all, because she had signed up as a student marshal for the extra credit. "What does that word even mean? Hypothesis?"

Easton opened his notebook to the page where he had looked it up for the board. "It comes from ancient Greek," he said. "It literally means putting or placing under."

Amina frowned. "Placing under? Under what?"

"That's what I asked. I thought I'd copied it wrong." He turned the notebook so she could see the printed page. "A hypothesis is something you place under your experiment. Like a foundation. You build the test on top of it." He had read that three times in his kitchen, the window open, a train horn far off, before it finally clicked.

"So yours was placed under and then crushed," Kiaan said, grinning.

"Basically." Easton looked at the little LED, still burning, stubborn and orange. Here was the part he kept turning over: if he had never written the guess, he would have run the same test and gotten the same result. But he would not have felt the result land anywhere. The wrongness needed something to be wrong about. He wasn't sure yet whether that made the guessing worth it or just painful, and he didn't try to settle it while the judges were circling.

Mr. Gagnon stopped at his table and read the whole board, top to bottom, including the part where Easton had written in red marker: My hypothesis was overturned. The cheap battery lasted longer. Then he tapped the still-glowing LED with one finger, like ringing a tiny doorbell.

"That one," Easton said, "still hasn't quit."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
Lillian counted the broken toothpicks on the lab table and wrote down the number before she forgot it. The science fair was on Friday, and her bridge model still sagged in the middle like a tired hammock. Across the table, Teresa was supposed to be recording data, but she had filled the whole margin of the notebook with tiny spirals.

"Third trial," Lillian said, laying the last toothpick across the span. The bridge groaned and collapsed. Teresa didn't even look up.

That was the third time this week. Teresa, who last year had won the fair with a volcano she had rebuilt four times, now spent lunch in the library and flinched when the bell rang. Lillian wondered what had changed. It wasn't the project, because Teresa still knew every formula. It wasn't her family, because her little brother still waved at her through the gym window every Tuesday. Maybe it was something Lillian couldn't see at all, something running underneath like a wire inside the bridge.

On Thursday, Lillian tried a small test. She set a timer and simulated the fair, calling out like a judge would. "Contestant, explain your structure." Teresa's hands started shaking so hard she knocked over the glue bottle. She fled to the hallway, and Lillian found her sitting against the lockers with her knees pulled up.

"I'm not being dramatic over something trivial," Teresa said before Lillian could speak. "I keep telling myself it's just a bridge, it's just a crowd, but my heart pounds anyway. It's been like this since October. I couldn't even go to Angelica's party."

Lillian sat down beside her. "That's not trivial. That's a long time."

Teresa wiped her eyes. "My mom took me to a doctor last month. I told her everything, and she said it's an anxiety disorder. That's what it's called when the anxiety is really intense and it lasts a long time and it gets in the way of daily life." She picked at her sleeve. "Feeling anxious sometimes is normal. Everybody gets that. Mine just went past normal. The good part is it's treatable. I started seeing someone for it, and some days are already better."

"So it can get better," Lillian said slowly. It was like finding the actual weak joint in the bridge instead of guessing. "Then we build around it. Tomorrow I'll present our data, and you stand next to me and hold the notebook. If a judge asks you something, you can squeeze my elbow and I'll take it. Deal?"

"Deal," Teresa said, and almost smiled. "Also, your load is off center. That's why it keeps failing."

On Friday, Mr. Rossi paused at their table, nodded at the rebuilt span, and said it reminded him of his pension planning, "boring but sturdy, built to hold up for years." Teresa held the notebook steady through the whole presentation, and when the ribbons were handed out, theirs was red. Lillian felt the squeeze on her elbow, but this time Teresa was just pointing at the ribbon, saying, "Third place. We built that."

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Muscle soreness after an unfamiliar workout is usually worst 24 to 72 hours afterward, which is called delayed onset muscle soreness.
story:
Hayden pushed through the pool doors on Tuesday feeling like a champion, which lasted exactly until he reached the stairs to the bleachers and his legs announced they were on strike. He gripped the railing and took the steps sideways, like a crab in swim trunks.

"You too?" Alma said from three steps up, lowering herself with both hands on the rail. "Yesterday after tryouts I felt amazing. I walked home. I had a snack. I ruled the world." She winced as she sat down. "Now I can barely fold myself into a chair."

Brodie arrived behind them, walking like a robot with low batteries. "Do not make me laugh," he said. "Laughing uses my stomach." He lowered himself onto the bench in one careful motion, then looked around the pool with narrowed eyes. "Something weird is going on. Everyone who swam hard Monday is hobbling today. The kids who didn't come Monday are fine. Is the pool cursed? Did someone put a hex in the deep end?"

Hayden had been wondering the same thing, sort of, minus the hex. He watched the other swimmers, counting. His sister had complained once after her first soccer practice of the season, but not that night. It hit her the day after, and worse the day after that. "I think it's not the pool," he said slowly. "I think it's timing. The soreness shows up late. Like a delayed package."

"A delayed package of pain," Alma said. "Worst mail ever."

At that moment a kid named Theo, who had felt so great Monday evening that he'd done a victory lap around the parking lot, attempted to climb the block for warm-up and made a noise like a startled goose. Mr. Pérez, the coach, just nodded as if he'd seen this exact thing every season for twenty years. "Anyone who says the word 'delayed' today gets out of treading-water drills," he called, and then pretended he hadn't said anything.

"Dude," Alma whispered, poking Hayden's arm, which he felt everywhere. "What's the word for when it hits later like this? My mom said it once. Delayed onset something."

"Delayed onset muscle soreness," said a girl from the next row, without looking up from stretching her calves. "It's usually worst 24 to 72 hours after a workout your body isn't used to." She flexed one foot and grimaced. "So tomorrow might be even worse than today. Plan accordingly." She said it like a weather report, then hobbled off toward the blocks, deeply buoyant despite everything, practically floating on her own smugness.

Hayden tested the idea in his head like a math problem. Monday was the hard, unfamiliar workout. Tuesday was one day later, and half the pool was walking like penguins. So Wednesday and Thursday, days two and three, could be the peak of the disaster. Factor in the fact that today's tryout would give their muscles new work to complain about, and Friday's final cut might happen right when everyone's legs were at their most dramatic. Which meant the swimmers who paced themselves, who migrated to the easier lanes and saved their arms, would look fresh exactly when it counted.

"Okay," he said, standing up in stages like a collapsing tent in reverse. "New plan. We go hard enough to make the team today, but we save the hero stuff. Our real competition is Thursday, when everyone else is noodle-legged."

Alma saluted, which hurt her shoulder, which made Brodie laugh, which hurt his stomach, which made Theo laugh from the blocks, which made him wobble, which made the whole pool go briefly, gloriously quiet.

"Steady," Mr. Pérez said, but he was smiling.

Hayden took the stairs down one careful crab-step at a time.

activity: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
knowledge_domain: the difference between a scientific claim backed by tested evidence and a story about one person's experience
fact: Before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors, a process called peer review.
story:
At his grandmother's backyard party, Owen sat at the wobbly card table with his cousin Jamie, scrolling through his phone while the grown-ups argued about the potato salad. Jamie had shown him a blog post claiming that a certain mushroom supplement could cure headaches in three days, because the writer's uncle had tried it and felt better. "See?" Jamie said. "Proof."

Owen wanted to believe it, because his mother got headaches all the time and he hated watching her lie down in the dark after work. But something bothered him. "One guy feeling better isn't really proof," he said. "Maybe his headache was going away anyway." Jamie rolled his eyes and stole a chip.

Across the yard, their neighbor Mr. Dang was grilling burgers, and Owen drifted over to him, since Mr. Dang worked at the university and always wore a T-shirt with a skeleton on it. "If someone writes something online," Owen asked, "how do you know if it's actually science?" Mr. Dang flipped a patty and squinted. "Depends where it's published. A blog is just one person typing. But before most scientific papers are published in a journal, other experts in the field review them for errors." He snapped his tongs. "It's called peer review." Then he went back to arguing with Owen's uncle about charcoal.

Owen had an idea. He walked back to the table and told Jamie they should look up the mushroom thing in an actual journal, not just the blog. They found the library's database on Owen's phone, and after some clumsy searching they found a real paper about the same supplement. The study had tested it on lots of people, not just one uncle, and the results showed it barely did anything for headaches. Owen felt a small, flat disappointment, but also something like satisfaction, the way a puzzle piece clicks even when the picture isn't what you hoped.

"So the blog guy just assumed it worked because of his uncle," Jamie said slowly, chewing the chip. Owen nodded. "And his motivation was probably selling the supplement. There was a link to buy it at the bottom." Jamie looked at his phone like it had tricked him personally.

Later, when everyone gathered around the picnic table for watermelon, Owen's mother asked what they'd been doing all afternoon. Before Owen could answer, Jamie said, "Owen proved that mushroom thing is fake." "We didn't prove anything," Owen said, cutting himself a slice. "The journal people checked it first. We just read it." His mother raised an eyebrow, and the aunts, in rare unanimous agreement, declared the watermelon excellent this year. Owen slid the biggest piece onto his mother's plate.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: Sweat cools the body as it evaporates, so in humid weather, when sweat evaporates slowly, athletes cool down less well and overheat more easily.
story:
Dylan's backyard was too small for a real field, so he and Zaynab had marked out goals with laundry baskets at either end of the grass. It was the last week of July, and the air felt like a wet towel pressed against his face. He dribbled around Zaynab anyway, shot, and watched the ball skim the basket and roll into the hedge.

"Rematch Saturday," Zaynab said, flopping onto the porch steps. "But I'm dead. We only played twenty minutes."

Dylan sat down beside her, shirt soaked, though he'd barely sprinted. That was the strange part. Last August he remembered a practice in Texas at his cousin's house where the thermometer read higher, and he'd felt tired but fine afterward. Today felt worse than that, and cooler. He turned the idea over while a cicada droned somewhere in the maple.

At Saturday's game, the problem returned with company. Simona, who usually ran the whole field twice without stopping, kept her hands on her knees at halftime, her face flushed. Dylan's own head ached in a dull, steady way. The other team, their usual adversary from across town, looked just as wrecked, so at least it was even.

The next morning Dylan decided to invest an hour in figuring it out. He spread a damp dish towel over the porch rail in the thick morning air and a second damp towel on a chair inside the air-conditioned kitchen. He checked them every ten minutes. The indoor towel went stiff and dry first. The outdoor one stayed limp, cool to the touch but dripping long after. He didn't have a name for what he was watching, but he could see that something in the sticky air was slowing the towels down.

"You look like a scientist," Zaynab said, arriving for practice with a water bottle the size of a fire extinguisher.

"Watch this." He held up both towels. "The one inside dried in half the time. Same water, same kind of towel. The wet air outside is the difference." He rubbed his forearm, still damp from an hour ago. "Sweat's the same. It cools you when it dries off you. When the air's already full of water, it dries slow, so it barely cools you at all. That's why we die out there even when it's not the hottest day."

"So the Texas practice," Zaynab said slowly.

"Dry air. The sweat dried fast. It was hotter but it worked better." He was already changing his mind about the week's plan. No more full-field scrimmages in August humidity. Short drills, long shade breaks, cold water on the wrists. Maybe even practice in the evening, when the air sometimes thinned out.

From the fence, Mr. Aydın, who had been watering his tomatoes in a slow, indifferent drift that wet half of Dylan's lawn as well, called over, "You two should be drinking more of that."

"We figured that out," Dylan said. He tossed Zaynab the ball, backing toward the basket goal. "First one to three, then we sit in the shade like sensible people."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
The cultural center smelled like cardamom and hot oil, and Dominic stood near the door holding his mother's coat because she had gone to find his aunt among the crowd. Outside, a procession was forming for Vaisakhi, and he could hear drums beating somewhere down the block, deep thumps he felt in his ribs.

Dominic wanted to know why this day mattered so much, but he did not want to ask and look like the only one who did not know. He had tried reading a poster in the lobby, but it just showed a schedule. So he made a plan: if he stood near the stage where families gathered, someone would probably tell the story out loud, and he could listen without asking.

He found a spot beside a family from his school, and next to them stood Khloe from his math class. A small girl tugged her uncle's sleeve and said, "Why is everyone so happy today?" The uncle crouched down. "Vaisakhi is the day, in 1699, when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," he said. Khloe caught Dominic's eye and whispered, "That's the community of initiated Sikhs, I think. My dad told me once."

Dominic tested his idea again at the craft table, where Ernest was attempting a paper flag with orange and blue. "Did you hear that story too?" Dominic asked. Ernest shook his head, so Dominic repeated the uncle's words, and Ernest nodded slowly. "So that's why the procession stops at certain corners," Ernest said. "They're retelling it, like stations." Dominic had not thought of that. He felt a small flush of pride that his listening had worked, and also a little embarrassed that he had been biased against asking in the first place, assuming everyone else had been born knowing things he had to hunt down.

They followed the procession out onto the street, where the drums got louder and the crowd spilled past the storefronts like a river pushing past its banks, a frontier of orange fabric moving down the block. Khloe walked with them, and the three of them stopped at each corner where the procession paused. Dominic noticed that people who knew the story explained it to people who did not, freely, without anyone having to disclose that they were confused.

At the last corner, the small girl from before ran up to Dominic and held out a piece of sweet she had been given, an extra one. "You were listening to my uncle too," she said. "He tells it the best." Dominic took the sweet and said, "He really does." The drums rolled again, and the whole street surged forward together.

activity: competing in a spelling bee
knowledge_domain: competing in a spelling bee
fact: Knowing a word's language of origin can help with spelling: the 'k' sound in 'chorus' is spelled 'ch' because it comes from Greek, while the 'sh' in 'chef' comes from French.
story:
The classroom smelled like whiteboard marker and nervous kid, and Wyatt was one of the nervous kids. Twelve spellers stood in a line at the front while Mr. Crowchild shuffled his index cards at the podium. Nylah leaned over from the next spot and whispered, "You look like you're about to be launched into space."

"I'm fine," Wyatt whispered back, which was a lie. He had studied every night for two weeks, and last night his dad had said, "Consider it income, all those words you're banking," which had made sense only because Wyatt was saving up for a new bike.

The first three rounds knocked out half the line. Saanvi got out on "raspberry," missing the silent p, and sat down at a desk in the front row with her arms crossed, watching like a hawk. Then it was just Wyatt, a kid from another class, and Nylah, who breezed through "picnic" like it was her own name.

"Chorus," said Mr. Crowchild. "Language of origin: Greek."

Wyatt opened his mouth and then closed it. The k sound. K? C? Something else? He assumed the k sound was always spelled with a k or a c, but wait. Greek. His brain flipped back to the study list, where "chorus" had sat next to "chaos," and he'd noticed both started with a ch that sounded like k. Both from Greek. So Greek words used ch for that sound, and this word was Greek, so it probably started with ch. He was guessing, but it was a guess with a shape to it.

"C-h-o-r-u-s. Chorus."

"Correct," said Mr. Crowchild, and Wyatt let out a breath that had been waiting in his chest since Tuesday.

Next round, Nylah got "chef." Mr. Crowchild said, "Language of origin: French." Nylah frowned, spelled it with a k, and sat down next to Saanvi with a groan. She pointed a finger at Wyatt. "Wait. You did the same sound in chorus with a ch. Why does yours work and mine doesn't?"

"It's the French," Wyatt said, still working it out as he said it. "The sh in 'chef' comes from French. The k sound in 'chorus' is spelled ch because it comes from Greek. French spells it sh, Greek spells it ch." Nylah stared at him, then laughed, which was better than the glare he'd been expecting.

"That's ridiculous. That's actually brilliant. I'm mad I didn't know that."

"One more word and we're done," said Mr. Crowchild, holding up the final card. His face was neutral, but his eyes had that glint teachers get when they know they've got a good one. Wyatt planted his feet and waited.

"Monarch," said Mr. Crowchild. "Language of origin: Greek."

activity: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
knowledge_domain: to test whether a solution is an acid or a base using litmus paper and the pH scale
fact: Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark.
story:
Alexandre unfolded the card table in the gymnasium and set out twelve little cups, each one labeled in his neatest handwriting: lemon juice, soap water, vinegar, baking soda mix, cola, and seven more. His poster read THE INVISIBLE COLOR OF CHEMICALS, and beside it sat a stack of thin strips that looked like scraps of purple paper. The judge would come by at ten thirty, which gave him forty minutes to fix his problem: three of his samples were turning the strips the wrong color, and he had no idea why.

"You look like your project is fighting you," said Sehaj, leaning over from the next table, where a volcano oozed baking-soda foam onto a tray.

"It is." Alexandre held up two strips, one pink, one blue. "I tested the soap twice and got two different answers. If I can't trust the paper, I can't trust anything on my table."

Sehaj picked up a strip and turned it over. "Where did you even get these?"

"Ms. Girma lent me the pack from the science room." Alexandre stopped. Ms. Girma had also lent him a book about indicators, which he had shoved in his backpack and never opened. He dug it out now, and Isa, who had wandered over from her table about magnets, read the page he flipped to out loud. "Litmus is a dye extracted from lichens, the crusty growths found on rocks and tree bark."

"Lichens?" Isa said. "Like that scratchy gray stuff on my grandma's garden wall? That's in this paper?"

Alexandre looked at the strip in his hand and felt the whole problem turn over in his mind. The paper wasn't some factory chemical with rules he couldn't see. It came from something growing on rocks and bark, and if it was a living dye, maybe it could go stale, or get damp, or be damaged by heat. He had kept the strips in his back pocket all morning while he carried his boxes. His own body heat and sweat could have ruined a few without leaving any mark he could see.

He laid out a test. From the borrowed pack he took six fresh strips he had never handled, using tweezers from the art kit Isa carried. He tested the soap again, twice, with fresh strips and with the pocket-warmed ones. The fresh strips both turned blue. The pocket ones gave him the scrambled answers. "It's not the soap," he said. "It's me. I cooked the strips."

"So the invisible thing wasn't the acid," Isa said slowly. "It was the damage you couldn't see either."

When Ms. Girma stopped at his table with her clipboard, he walked her through it, and he even advocated labeling every kit "keep strips cool and dry," since half the class would probably carry them in pockets too. She wrote something down and smiled. Alexandre won a red ribbon, third place, behind Isa's magnets and Sehaj's volcano.

After the fair, his mother picked him up early so they could stop by his grandfather's house. Waiting at the gate, Alexandre ran his thumb over the crusty gray growths on the garden wall and thought about how much of chemistry seemed to be like this: rules you couldn't watch working, causes you had to corner with a test, and the insight that the proportional effort of one careful morning of checking your tools was worth more than an afternoon of guessing. The wall was damp where a sprinkler had sprayed it. He peeled a tiny fleck of lichen loose, folded it into his notebook, and put the notebook in his front pocket, where he promised himself it would stay cool and dry.

At the ribbon ceremony, Sehaj had slipped Alexandre's own pocket-warmed strips into the cup labeled lemon juice, so Alexandre's display card, photographed by the local paper, showed vinegar turning blue and lemon juice turning pink under a heading that read, "Student masters the pH scale." The photographer looked at his camera, looked at the table, and said, "Kid, that's the best one I've seen all day."

activity: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
knowledge_domain: to recognise signs of stress and use deep breathing and sleep routines to manage it
fact: In belly breathing, also called diaphragmatic breathing, the belly rises as you breathe in instead of the shoulders lifting, which lets the lungs fill more deeply.
story:
Willow had wanted to sign up for the ropes course on the first day of camp, but by Thursday she still hadn't climbed higher than the second rung. Every time she looked up at the platform, her heart pounded so hard she could feel it in her ears, and she told the coach her harness felt loose even when it didn't.

At dinner in the mess hall, she pushed around the camp cuisine, which everyone agreed was not authentic anything, just noodles and mystery stew. Nathaniel sat down across from her with his tray. "You froze again today," he said. "Same as Tuesday."

"I despise that course," Willow said, though that wasn't quite true, and she knew it. What she despised was the shaky, breathless feeling that took her over at the bottom of the ladder. She tried to picture the last three attempts, looking for a pattern. On Tuesday her shoulders had been up near her ears. Wednesday, same thing. "Nathaniel, put your hand on your stomach and take a breath," she said suddenly.

He raised an eyebrow but did it. "Okay. Now what?"

"Watch your shoulders too." Willow put her own hand on her belly and breathed in. Her shoulders rose; her stomach stayed flat. His did the same. "We're breathing wrong," she said. "Mr. Lindqvist said one word to me after the swim test, belly breathing, but I didn't listen."

Mr. Lindqvist ran the waterfront, and that evening Willow found him coiling rope by the dock. "Is belly breathing where your stomach goes out instead of your shoulders going up?" she asked.

"That's the one," he said, and went back to his rope.

Willow and Nathaniel practiced on the bunk porch until lights-out. On the tenth try, her belly finally rose while her shoulders stayed still, and the breath felt longer, deeper, like it actually reached somewhere. She made herself do it slowly ten times in her sleeping bag, and for the first time all week she fell asleep before the crickets quit.

Friday morning she stood at the ladder again. Halfway up, her heart started hammering, and she felt her shoulders creeping toward her ears. She stopped, hung there, put one hand flat against her belly, and breathed in until her stomach pushed against her palm. Three breaths. Her shoulders dropped. She climbed the last four rungs and pulled herself onto the platform, where Nathaniel was already waiting.

"Figured it out," he said.

"Still figuring," Willow said, and looked down at the lake.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: Blushing happens when blood vessels in the face widen and let more blood flow near the skin.
story:
Emilia checked her reflection in the concession stand window for the third time since kickoff. Behind her, the whole crowd groaned as the away team scored, but she barely noticed, because Terrance was walking toward her with two hot chocolates and a nervous grin that matched her own.

"You made it," he said, handing her one. "I thought maybe you'd bail."

"Bail? I've been planning this since Tuesday." As soon as she said it, she regretted it. Too eager. But Terrance laughed, a real laugh, and then she felt something worse than regret: her whole face heating up like a stove left on.

She turned toward the field fast. "Great defense," she muttered, to nobody.

Brooklyn appeared beside her with a foam finger and no mercy. "Your face is the color of a stop sign."

"I know." Emilia kept her eyes on the game. She had read something months ago in a science magazine in Ms. Pham's classroom, and now she was trying to piece it back together. Blushing was blood, she remembered that much. Something about blood vessels widening, letting more blood flow near the skin. That was why faces turned red, and why, she reasoned, pressing something cold against her cheeks might shrink that flow back down. She tested the idea immediately, pressing the hot chocolate cup against her cheek even though it was warm and made everything worse.

"Smooth," Brooklyn said.

"Shut up. It was worth a try."

By the start of the fourth quarter, the score was tied and the crowd had gotten loud, everyone sensing the game climbing toward its climax. Emilia had stopped trying to hide every blush. When Terrance joked that her cheering had probably frightened the quarterback into fumbling, she laughed, went red again, and just let him see it.

"You do that a lot," he said, not unkindly.

"Blushing? Yeah. It means the blood vessels in my face are widening, letting more blood flow near the skin." She shrugged. "Apparently my face can't keep a secret."

Terrance turned red himself. "Huh. Mine too, then."

The clock wound down, and with eleven seconds left the home team kicked the winning field goal. The stands exploded, and Terrance, catching her hand in the chaos of everyone standing and screaming, held on even after the noise faded. The scoreboard lights blinked. Her cheeks burned, and this time she didn't turn away.

"Hot chocolate rematch next Friday?" he asked.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: Practicing in several shorter sessions spread over days usually builds a skill better than the same total time crammed into one long session.
story:
Isaac had four days to learn the trumpet solo for Friday's assembly, and one Saturday free. He spread his music on the bed, looked at the clock, and decided to do all two hours at once. He played the same sixteen measures until his lips buzzed, then played them again. By dinnertime he could get through the solo, mostly.

On Monday, in the music classroom, his lips had gone soft again. Mr. Chen set the metronome ticking and Isaac fumbled the same passage, the one with the tricky leap up to the high G. Mr. Chen just said, "Again." Isaac missed it again.

"You sounded fine Saturday," Isaac told Karl after class. Karl had heard him through his bedroom wall all weekend.

"Fine how?" Karl said. "You played it, like, forty times in a row."

Isaac thought about that on the walk home. Forty times in a row, and now it was gone. He thought about how he had learned his locker combination last fall. He hadn't drilled it for an hour. He'd tried it once each morning, and by Thursday his hand knew it without looking. Maybe the same total time worked differently if he split it up.

So he ran a test on himself. He still had two hours left before Friday, so he parceled it out: twenty minutes Monday night, twenty Tuesday, twenty Wednesday, twenty Thursday. Each night the passage started rough, then came back faster than the night before. By Thursday's session he hit the high G on the second try, then every try after that.

Loukas, who sat first trumpet, had his own problem. He'd been cramming his scales the night before every lesson and kept stumbling on the same ones. Isaac mentioned what he'd tried, keeping it short. Loukas shrugged, but on Wednesday he showed up at Isaac's desk. "I did fifteen minutes a night instead of one big block. Same total time, I checked. It's better. That's annoying, actually." Isaac just grinned and kept packing his bag.

Friday came, and the gym filled with the whole school plus parents who'd bought tickets, since ticket revenue paid for the new risers the band needed. Isaac stood in the second row. When his sixteen measures arrived, his fingers moved before he had to think, and the high G came out clean and bright, hanging in the air over the gym.

Afterward, Mr. Chen found him by the doors. "That was a significant improvement since Monday. What changed?"

Isaac held up his trumpet case. "Short practice. Lots of days in a row."

"Good," said Mr. Chen. "Same time Monday."

Loukas elbowed him. "Told you it was annoying."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: The Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition, that lower rock layers are older, in 1669.
story:
Juliette had a talk to give on Monday about how a river carves a canyon, and she had exactly one idea: build a river in the kitchen sink. She layered sand, dirt from the flowerpot, and flour into a glass baking dish, pressing each layer flat. Flour on the bottom, sand in the middle, dirt on top. It looked like a sad dessert.

Zac arrived just as she turned on the faucet. "What are we supposed to be learning from this?" he asked, dragging a stool to the counter.

"Watch the water." She angled the dish so a thin stream cut across the layers. At first nothing happened, which was annoying. Then the stream found a low spot and began to chew into the top layer, carrying brown crumbs downstream in a muddy plume. Where the water slowed at the far end, the crumbs settled into a tiny fan. "There," she said. "The river digs where it's fast and drops stuff where it's slow. It's erosion and deposition at the same time."

Zac leaned in. "Okay, but if it keeps cutting, it gets down to the sand. Then the flour. Then what?"

"Then I get in trouble for using all the flour." She watched the stream sink deeper, though, because he had a point. The canyon wasn't just getting wider. It was cutting through, top to bottom, like it was reading downward. She turned off the tap and got out her phone.

The search took a while because "rock layers pages" mostly gave her an ad for mattresses. But she found a museum page with a picture of striped rock and a sign that made her sit up straight. The sign said the Danish scientist Nicolas Steno published the law of superposition in 1669. "It's called the law of superposition," she read aloud, "and it means lower rock layers are older."

"Older," Zac repeated. "So the bottom of your dish, the flour, that's the oldest."

"The first thing down." She tapped the glass. "So when a river cuts a canyon, it's slicing through time. The bottom rock got there first, and everything else piled on top, layer by layer, and then the river came along and cut through all of it." She started the water again, slower this time, and they watched the stream work its way down one millimeter at a time.

"Can we incorporate something with more drama?" Zac said. "Like a rockslide?"

She set a pebble at the top of the stream. The water carved around it, split into two channels, and left the pebble sitting on a tiny island of dirt while everything downstream turned brown. "Fine," she said. "Nature's providing drama for free." On her notepad she wrote "pebble = million years, approximately," then crossed out "approximately" and wrote "definitely."

Her mother came in, looked at the counter, and adopted a neutral expression. "Is my herbivore in that dish?"

"One fossil snail," Juliette said solemnly, pressing a macaroni shell into the flour layer. "Bottom layer. Oldest one. Steno says so."

activity: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
knowledge_domain: to read the periodic table and find the number of protons in an element from its atomic number
fact: In a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons, so the atomic number also tells you how many electrons it has.
story:
The garage smelled like sawdust and old paint, and Maeva had claimed the workbench for the most important project of her life: a model of a sodium atom due Monday. Sebastien sat on an overturned crate, holding a shoebox full of Styrofoam balls they had painted the night before. "The glue gun's hot," he said. "How many electrons do we stick on?"

That was the problem. Maeva stared at the printout Ms. Yoon had given her, a periodic table squished onto one page. She had circled sodium, and she knew the big number 11 in its box was called the atomic number. Eleven protons, she had written in her notes. But the assignment said the model had to be a neutral atom, and she had no idea how many electrons that meant. She couldn't count them. Nobody could see electrons, that was the whole frustrating thing.

"You could just put a random amount," Sebastien said, testing the glue on a scrap of wood. "It's a model." Maeva said that if the numbers were random, the model wasn't science, it was decoration. She flipped the printout over, where she had copied the sentence Ms. Yoon had underlined on the board: in a neutral atom, the number of electrons equals the number of protons. She read it twice, then looked up so fast she nearly knocked over the paint water. "Sebastien. The atomic number is eleven. Eleven protons. So if it's neutral, it's eleven electrons too." The atomic number told you both.

"Prove it," Sebastien said, which was fair, because Maeva had been wrong about the beaker thing last week. She tried it on another element to test the idea. Carbon, atomic number six: six protons, so six electrons in a neutral atom. Oxygen, atomic number eight: eight and eight. The rule held every time she checked it, like a pattern hiding inside the table, waiting for her. She counted out eleven small balls and handed them to Sebastien. "Two go on the first ring," she said, "and the rest on the outer ones. That part's in the book."

From the doorway, Ms. Yoon, who had come across the yard to borrow a ladder, watched them glue the last electron into place. "You know," she said, "sodium's the one you isolate from salt, and it will actually ignite if you drop it in water." Sebastien leaned back from the model. "Venomous?" he asked. "Not exactly," Ms. Yoon said, laughing. Maeva turned the finished atom slowly in her hands, all eleven electrons in their rings, and carried it toward the house, holding it level like something that really might ignite.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Ritardando, often written rit., means gradually slowing down, and accelerando means gradually speeding up.
story:
Hazel slid onto the piano bench in the music room and set the sheet music on the stand before anyone could grab the seat. Rehearsal didn't start for ten minutes, but she wanted to look at the spot in measure thirty-four one more time, the spot where the whole band had fallen apart yesterday.

"Move over," said Donovan, nudging her with his elbow. He balanced his trumpet case on the edge of the piano. "Ms. Yip wants me on the melody today, and my grandma is coming to the concert, so I can't sound like a dying goose."

She shifted to make room. Donovan talked about the concert every single day, and his grandmother had already promised to wear her good purple hat, which apparently was a big deal. "You won't sound like a goose," Hazel said. Then she pulled out the crumpled note she'd found taped to her locker that morning and smoothed it flat on the music stand.

Half the band slows down at the rit. and half doesn't, the note read. That's why it sounds like a train wreck. Not a trumpet problem. Signed, someone in the back row.

Donovan leaned over to read it. His shoulders dropped an inch, like a weight had come off them. "So it's not us?"

"It's the word." Hazel tapped measure thirty-four. "See this? Rit. It's telling us something." She'd noticed the pattern yesterday: the flutes and the low brass dragged behind the beat right at that measure, while the trumpets and percussion charged ahead. Two different speeds, one piece of music, total disaster. She had a guess about what the three letters meant, but she wanted to test it before she said anything out loud.

"Rit. means gradually slowing down," said Cody, appearing behind them with his drumsticks. He pointed at the marking. "And accelerando means gradually speeding up. They're basically opposites. My cousin told me when she took piano."

Hazel stared at the page. If rit. meant slowing down, then the players who were slowing were actually following the music correctly, and the ones who kept the old tempo were wrong. "So the fix isn't compromise," she said slowly. "The trumpets just have to come with us. We slow, they slow. All together, bit by bit, not all at once."

When Ms. Yip raised her baton, Hazel caught Donovan's eye and tapped the sheet music, then made a slow sinking motion with her hand. He grinned and passed it along the trumpet section like a secret. At measure thirty-four the whole band eased back together, note by note, like a wave rolling onto a beach and settling into sand. Cody's drumsticks followed them down gently instead of charging ahead, reckless and loud as they had been all week. For the first time, the ending of the piece sounded like an ending.

Ms. Yip lowered her baton and blinked at them. "Well," she said. "Whatever you did, do it again."

Donovan's grandma was going to hear something worth the purple hat. Hazel turned the page and set her fingers on the keys, ready to go again.

activity: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
knowledge_domain: to paint a portrait in watercolour by layering washes from light to dark
fact: Painting wet-on-wet, putting paint onto paper that is still wet, makes the colour spread with soft, blurry edges instead of crisp ones.
story:
Aaron had ruined four portraits since Monday, and camp ended on Saturday. Ms. Visser's art shed smelled like lake water and old paper, and every afternoon Aaron sat at the wobbly table trying to paint his grandfather's face. The problem was simple and terrible: he kept painting the skin in one thick coat, and it came out flat as a paper plate.

"You're doing it backwards," said Micaela, leaning over from the next easel. "Ms. Visser said light to dark. Like, the pale wash is the foundation, and you add darker layers on top for the shadows."

Aaron looked at his paper plate grandfather. "So the light stuff goes on first."

"Obviously. You've been going dark to light like some kind of cave painter."

He retrieved a fresh sheet from the supply shelf, taped it down, and mixed a pale peach wash, so pale it looked like water pretending to be paint. He brushed it over the whole oval of the face. Then, because he was impatient, he loaded his brush with a darker tone for the shadow under the jaw and touched it straight onto the wet paper.

The shadow did not stay a shadow. It bloomed outward like a drop of juice in a glass of milk, edges going fuzzy, crawling across the cheek. Aaron yelped and grabbed a paper towel, which smeared everything into a pink cloud.

"Whoa," said Parker from the window, where he was supposed to be sketching but was mostly watching other people fail. "It spread like a rumour."

Aaron stared at the cloud. His first four failures had been crisp and flat. This one was blurry, but soft, almost like real skin in bad light. He thought about it while the paper dried. The paint had spread because the paper was still wet. That was the only thing different. On his ruined sheets before, the paper had been dry each time he added a layer, so every edge stayed hard. He needed hard edges for the eyes and the mouth. But for skin, for cheeks and shadow, soft might actually be right.

"Wet-on-wet," he said, mostly to himself. "That's what it did."

"What's what did?" said Parker.

"Paint on paper that's still wet. It spreads out all blurry."

He tried again. Pale foundation wash first. Then, while the paper still shone with damp, he touched the shadow tone under the jaw and let it bloom. It made a soft gray pool, not a line, exactly like shadow on a real face. For the eyes he waited until the paper was dry, and those came out crisp and dark. It was a system. It was, he thought, almost a cheat code.

By Friday the portrait was passable. Micaela said it looked like his grandfather had been sitting in fog, but nice fog. Parker said it looked like his grandfather was dreaming, which Aaron decided to take as a compliment. When Ms. Visser walked past, he covered it with his hands, then moved them, quick, before he could lose his nerve.

She looked for a long moment. "The jaw shadow," she said. "Do that again."

Aaron picked up his brush.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A reverse image search can show where a photo appeared online before, which can reveal that an old picture is being passed off as new.
story:
Eleanor leaned over Dillon's phone just as the lunch bell rang, but nobody moved toward the door. A flood photo was spreading across every feed in the eighth grade: brown water swallowing a parking lot, a car with only its roof showing, a caption in red letters that said BREAKING. "My mom says they might cancel school tomorrow," Dillon said. "My uncle shared it too, and he never shares anything."

"Where did it come from?" Eleanor asked. Dillon shrugged. "It's news, it's everywhere." That answer sat wrong with her, the way a wobbly lab stool sits wrong. Everyone was repeating the picture, but nobody was saying who took it, or where, or when. She wondered how you could check a thing like that, when the photo itself was the only evidence anyone had.

Mr. Foster had left the classroom computers on for the robotics club, but the club's rule was supposed to restrict the machines to club members until three o'clock. Eleanor glanced at the clock. Twelve minutes until the club arrived and Mr. Foster came back. "Lyam," she whispered, "come here. You too, Dillon. Quick." She dragged the photo off Dillon's phone onto the nearest screen and stared at it. "A picture is just information," she muttered. "Information can be searched."

Lyam leaned in. "Searched how? You can't type a picture." "You can, actually," Eleanor said. "My cousin showed me last summer. A reverse image search. You give it the picture instead of words, and it shows you where that photo appeared online before." She pulled up the search page, chose the image option, and dropped the file in. The three of them watched the little spinning circle, and Eleanor's heart thumped like it did before a timer went off in a lab.

Results loaded. The same parking lot, the same half-drowned car, on a weather site from years back. The photo had appeared online long before today, attached to an old story about a different storm entirely. "So it's not breaking anything," Lyam said slowly. "It's an old picture being passed off as new." Dillon groaned. "I texted my mom. And my uncle. And, um, basically everyone I know." The clock showed four minutes left, so the three of them typed fast, forwarding the search results, undoing shares where they could.

Mr. Foster walked in at three o'clock sharp, carrying his coffee, and raised an eyebrow at the three of them crowded around a club computer. "Robots aren't until Thursday," he said. Eleanor explained about the flood photo, the reverse search, the old weather page. He nodded, almost smiling. "Good thinking. Though I have to tell you, school was never going to be canceled. There's no flood." He pointed out the window, where the parking lot stood bone dry under an ordinary gray sky. "That's the real evidence." Dillon looked at his phone, where his uncle had just replied with a thumbs up and the words, "Stay safe, kiddo," and Eleanor started to laugh.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: Loaded words carry strong feelings beyond their plain meaning, so calling the same crowd "protesters" or "rioters" can push readers toward opposite opinions.
story:
Livia spread the laptop, a bag of chips, and three sodas across the coffee table, and Phoebe and Abbey sank into the couch on either side of her. Their news project was due Friday, and Ms. Müller had told them only one thing: find two stories about the same event and figure out what the stories were really doing. Livia clicked open the first headline, which read "Thousands March for Clean Water," and beneath it a photo of families holding painted signs. The second headline, from a different site, read "Rioters Disrupt Downtown Overnight," and its photo showed broken glass on a sidewalk.

"That's the same day," Abbey said, leaning closer. "Same street corner, even. Look at the bank sign in both pictures."

Phoebe read the first story aloud, and everyone agreed the marchers sounded brave and reasonable. Then she read the second, and Livia noticed her own stomach tightening as if the crowd had turned dangerous in the space of one paragraph. "Wait," she said. "Same people, same street. Why do I feel two different things?" She underlined marchers in blue and rioters in red, then underlined every word that made her feel something: brave, reckless, angry, proud. The page began to look like it had a rash.

"They're loaded words," Phoebe said slowly. "Like, they carry feelings beyond what they plain mean. The same crowd can be protesters or rioters, and that one word pushes you toward opposite opinions." Livia tested it. She covered the word rioters with her thumb and read the sentence again, and the crowd in her head quieted down, just standing there, neither heroes nor monsters. She tried it with marchers too, and the halo around them faded as well. It was like watching a larva turn out to be a caterpillar, one thing the whole time, wearing different skins.

"Look at these ads too," Abbey said, scrolling the sidebar of the second site. A famous actor grinned beside a bottle of vitamins, saying everyone he knew was taking them, and below that a banner claimed nine out of ten households had already switched brands. "Why does it matter that a movie star takes vitamins?" Livia asked. "He doesn't know anything about pills." Abbey shrugged. "And the nine out of ten thing makes you feel like the odd one out if you say no."

Livia pulled out her phone and typed a message to Ms. Müller: "We found two headlines about the same water march and the words alone made us disagree with each other. Are we on the right track or did we embarrass ourselves?" While they waited, she copied both headlines onto poster board, leaving a blank space between them where the crowd could be anything. The phone buzzed on the table. Phoebe grabbed the marker and held it over the blank space. "So what do we write there?" she asked. "The actual word, or no word at all?"

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: Ringing in the ears after loud music, called tinnitus, is a warning sign that the ears were exposed to noise loud enough to damage hearing.
story:
Jace stood in Hassan's kitchen, holding a blue tie in one hand and a paper tag in the other. The dance started in two hours, and the tie still had its tag because Jace had never worn one before.

"You look like you're defusing a bomb," Hassan said, grabbing the tie. "My dad supervises half the chaperones tonight, so he practiced knots on me last week. Pay attention."

Hassan's little sister, Emmie, wandered in with a scavenger hunt list she'd made for herself, hunting through drawers for a rubber band, a penny, and something blue. "Something blue," she announced, pointing at Jace's tie. "You're on my list."

Jace laughed, but his stomach was tight. He'd told his mom he didn't care about the dance, which wasn't true. What he wanted was for Nia Fernandez to see him there, not hiding by the water fountain like last year at the fall social, when he'd spent the whole night near a speaker stack so loud his ears buzzed until Sunday. He'd stood there because it was the darkest corner, and dark corners felt safe.

Hassan looped the knot and cinched it. "There. Distinguished. Like a mayor."

They walked to school together through the dilapidated lot behind the gym, where the old fence leaned and weeds grew through the cracked asphalt. Bass thumped from inside before they even reached the doors.

The gym was a wall of noise. The DJ had set up his speakers at one end, and the crowd pressed closest there, right against the wall of sound. Jace's old habit said go stand there, disappear into the loud dark. Instead he watched. Kids near the speakers were shouting at each other, not talking. A girl by the water fountain was chatting normally. He moved toward the fountain, and Nia ended up beside him while they both waited for a turn. They talked about the terrible punch, and then about nothing important, for almost an hour. It was the best bad punch he'd ever had.

That night, lying on his floor at home, Jace noticed the quiet in his ears. Last year after the fall social, a high thin ringing had followed him for days, like a mosquito that wouldn't leave. This night, nothing. Just quiet. He remembered his doctor mentioning, back when his mom dragged him in for that ringing, that it even had a name. "Tinnitus," she'd said, writing it on a card for him, and told him it was a warning sign the ears had been hit by noise loud enough to damage hearing. He'd stuffed the card in a drawer and forgotten it.

He pulled the card out now. He hadn't thought about it once at the dance, but he must have done something right anyway, standing back from all that thumping.

At the next dance, he thought, he'd try the fountain side again. Maybe he'd even ask Nia to save him a spot. He put the card on his nightstand, next to the paper tag from the tie, and turned off the light.

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: Italian tempo words describe speed: largo means very slow, andante means at a walking pace, and allegro means fast and lively.
story:
The basement of the old synagogue smelled like dust and candle wax, and the piano in the corner hadn't been tuned since anyone could remember. Violet sat down anyway, because tonight was the Hanukkah concert rehearsal and she was playing the solo in the middle of the piece. She had only six days to learn it.

Ms. Karimi had handed out the sheet music on Sunday, then gone home with a fever, so the rehearsal was just Violet and her friends Jan and Brogan, who would sing the second part. At the top of the page sat three strange words: largo at the beginning, andante in the middle, allegro at the end. Brogan leaned over her shoulder and squinted. "Those are Italian, I think. My cousin invests in opera tickets, he says Italian is everywhere in music."

"Probably just decoration," Jan said, shrugging.

Violet decided andante sounded the most impressive, like something fast and brilliant, and she played the middle section that way, flying through the runs at top speed. The whole thing collapsed. Her fingers tangled, Jan came in at the wrong moment, and the final chord landed like a dropped tray of dishes. Brogan laughed so hard he knocked over a folding chair. "That was predatory," he gasped. "Like a hawk attacking the keyboard."

Violet stared at the page, her ears still hot. Last spring she had skipped reading the rules of the science fair too, and her volcano had erupted sideways onto a judge's clipboard. She had promised herself she would stop guessing and start looking things up, and here she was, guessing again. "There's a dictionary in the office upstairs," she said. "The rabbi keeps one next to the prayer books."

She found it and carried it back down, flipping pages while Jan held the flashlight on her phone. The entries were short. Largo: very slow. Andante: at a walking pace. Allegro: fast and lively. So the words were instructions about speed, not decoration at all, and she had played the whole middle backwards, slow where it should walk and fast where it should crawl. No wonder it fell apart.

They tried it again, this time with Violet dragging the opening out until it felt almost too long, letting the middle stroll, then letting the end run. Something clicked. The melody rose out of the untuned piano like it had been waiting there the whole time. Jan's voice settled into it, and even Brogan stopped joking and hummed along.

When Violet hit the last chord, Ms. Karimi was standing at the bottom of the stairs, still pale, coat over her pajamas. She had come to check on them despite the fever. She listened to the ending echo off the stone walls and nodded slowly. "Play the largo even slower," she said. "Make them wait for it."

activity: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
knowledge_domain: to explain how nicotine causes addiction in the brain's reward pathway
fact: Nicotine causes brain cells in the reward pathway to release dopamine, a chemical messenger linked to pleasure and motivation.
story:
Hunter's table at the camp science fair had a shoebox, three marbles, and a hand-drawn map of the brain that his little cousin could have done better. He had signed up to explain why his grandpa had struggled for ten years to quit smoking, and so far the only person who had stopped at his table was Mira, and she had only come to steal his duct tape.

"It looks naive," Mira said, tapping the drawing. "Like a potato drew it."

"It's a prototype," Hunter said. "That means a first version." He pointed at a pathway he had colored gold, running from the front of the brain to the middle. "This is the reward pathway. Watch." He rolled a marble down a groove so it struck a lever, and the lever flipped a paper flap that read FEELS GOOD. "That's what nicotine does. It hits the cells in there and they release dopamine."

"What's dopamine?" Gia had wandered over, chewing a granola bar.

"A chemical messenger," Hunter said. "Linked to pleasure and motivation." He rolled the marble again, and the flap flipped again. "The brain likes it. So the brain wants it again. Grandpa said that's why quitting was the hardest thing he ever did. His brain kept asking."

Gia frowned at the shoebox. "But you can't see any of that happening. It's all inside."

"That's the problem," Hunter admitted. His first plan had been to saw a skull in half, but the camp director, Mr. Saleh, had said no. So Hunter had spent the evening trying to make something invisible visible. The marble was his best idea so far, and it rolled crooked every third time.

Mr. Saleh stopped at the table, arms crossed. "Elaborate," he said. "Show me more than one roll."

Hunter took a breath. He grabbed a second marble, then a third, and rolled them one after another, faster and faster, until the flap was flipping like a startled bird. FEELS GOOD, FEELS GOOD, FEELS GOOD. "See? The brain gets the message over and over, and it starts to expect it. Grandpa said that after a while his brain panicked when the marbles stopped." He let the last marble roll and settle, and the flap hung still.

A knot of campers had gathered. One kid asked whether coffee did that, and Hunter said he honestly didn't know, which made Mr. Saleh nod like Hunter had said something brilliant. Gia borrowed a marble and rolled it herself, then rolled it again, and again, and then a fourth time.

"Okay, that's mine now," Gia said, pocketing the marble.

"You're proving my whole point," Hunter said. "You can't stop."

"Exactly." Gia grinned and held the marble up to the light. "Now I know how your grandpa felt. Except my dopamine is blue and costs nothing."

Mr. Saleh pinned a blue ribbon on the potato-brain drawing and reached past Gia to pocket a second marble for himself.
